paper_metadata.title: Space and Time Cost of Continuous Rotations in Surface Codes

summary: The paper performs a surface‑code resource analysis of continuous rotation implementations using catalyst towers. For an option‑pricing phase oracle (S=36, n=15), independent catalyst towers reduce measurement depth to 17 steps compared with 32 for gate synthesis, and can lower spacetime volume up to code distance ≈13. For Gaussian state preparation (2100 rotations), catalyst towers reduce expected T‑count per repetition from 53,024 (gate synthesis) to 28,709 with an expected RUS depth of 39.

experiments.description: Surface-code resource analysis of low-depth parallel piecewise phase oracle circuits for option pricing, comparing gate synthesis, in-circuit catalyst towers, and independent catalyst towers.

algorithm.variant: low-depth parallel piecewise phase oracle with catalyst towers

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Phase oracle implements |x⟩ -> exp(i f(x))|x⟩ using a parallel piecewise circuit with fan-out/fan-in and repeated rotations; no QUBO encoding.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Implement a phase oracle for option pricing subroutines with minimal space-time cost.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Parallel fan-out/fan-in, logical-AND gates, AutoCCZ magic states, and catalyst towers; no penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: Derivative-pricing / option-pricing phase oracle subroutine used inside amplitude estimation.

dataset_specification.description: Option pricing parameter setting taken from prior work; piecewise function with S=36 segments and n=15 input qubits.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical resource estimation across increasing code distance; comparison of physical qubit count and spacetime volume for three rotation-implementation strategies.

transpilation_settings.routing_method: lattice surgery / long-range CNOT via ref. [24]

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Fan-out via local GHZ-state preparation; option-pricing parameters from prior work.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Resource comparison over code distance; no numerical optimization reported.

speedup_claims.factor: lower spacetime volume than conventional gate synthesis up to code distance ~13
speedup_claims.conditions: surface-code architecture; option-pricing phase oracle; low-to-medium code distances; S=36, n=15, p=1e-4; repeated subroutine use
speedup_claims.caveats: At code distances above 16, direct gate synthesis appears to outperform the catalyst-tower methods in both space and spacetime volume.

speedup_claims.conditions: for code distances beyond the threshold region discussed in the paper
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states this as a speedup with a modest increase in spacetime volume; exact factor is approximate and application-specific.

speedup_claims.factor: logarithmic depth scaling in S and n
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a scaling claim, not a measured asymptotic proof for all settings.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Crossover in spacetime efficiency between methods occurs around surface-code distance ≈13 (independent towers vs gate synthesis) and ≈16 (gate synthesis becomes best).
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Fault‑tolerant surface‑code machine with code distances up to ~16+, ~10^8 T‑states, logical qubit counts defined by tower layouts, and large magic‑state distillation factories.
limiting_factors: Results depend strongly on routing overhead and distillation factory assumptions
No comparison against classical runtime for option pricing

notes: Hardware is a surface-code resource analysis, not a specific QPU run.
num_qubits is not given as a single total for the experiment; the paper reports logical-qubit formulas and physical-qubit estimates instead.
Measurement depths 32, 62, and 17 are explicitly reported for gate synthesis, in-circuit towers, and independent towers, respectively.
No asymptotic speedup vs classical is analyzed; only resource tradeoffs are compared.
Authors explicitly frame the work as a resource comparison between rotation-synthesis strategies rather than demonstrating quantum advantage.
Only analytical resource estimates are presented; no classical-vs-quantum performance comparison.

experiments.description: Surface-code resource analysis of repeated Gaussian-state preparation using variational Ry-CNOT circuits and independent catalyst towers, comparing control and excess tower schemes against conventional gate synthesis.

algorithm.variant: variational Ry-CNOT state preparation with catalyst towers
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Classically trained Ry-CNOT ansatz; parameters are the trained circuit angles from prior work.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Gaussian amplitudes are prepared by a variational Ry-CNOT circuit; continuous rotations are implemented via Rz(θ)=SHRz(θ)HS† identity.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Prepare multiple copies of a quantum state whose amplitudes follow a normal distribution.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Independent catalyst towers with RUS teleportation; control and excess schemes manage resource-state supply.

problem_instance.description: Preparation of 60 copies of a 5-qubit Gaussian state circuit used in derivative-pricing amplitude-estimation workflow.

dataset_specification.description: 60 parallel copies of a 5-qubit, 7-layer variational circuit with 35 Ry rotations each.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Classically trained state-preparation circuit; Gaussian target amplitudes.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical resource estimation; expected T-count and expected measurement depth estimated via numerical simulation with 10,000 samples for the RUS depth distribution.

transpilation_settings.routing_method: lattice surgery / long-range CNOT via ref. [24]

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classically trained variational circuit; produce-and-store strategy for resource states.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Resource comparison across code distance for gate synthesis vs control/excess independent towers.

speedup_claims.conditions: for code distances below 10; Gaussian state preparation with independent catalyst towers; excess scheme
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports this as an approximate factor and notes that the excess scheme uses more T-states but fewer logical qubits.

speedup_claims.factor: lower physical qubit count than gate synthesis
speedup_claims.conditions: for code distances below 10; excess scheme
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not provide a single numeric crossover point for physical qubit count in the text, only the qualitative comparison and a figure.

speedup_claims.factor: expected depth independent of RT and logarithmic in n
speedup_claims.conditions: independent catalyst towers with RUS teleportation
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a scaling statement; the paper also notes the resource-state preparation stage requires more measurement steps and motivates a produce-and-store strategy.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Independent catalyst towers outperform gate synthesis in qubit cost for code distances below ~10 in the Gaussian-state preparation example.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Fault‑tolerant surface‑code device with ~1200 logical data qubits plus thousands of logical qubits for routing, towers, and storage of ~4200 rotation resource states.
limiting_factors: Requires thousands of logical qubits and large routing overhead
Assumes produce-and-store strategy for resource states
Performance advantage only relative to alternative rotation synthesis methods, not classical algorithms

notes: The paper reports 5 qubits per circuit and 60 copies, but not a single total qubit count for the full layout; physical-qubit estimates are given instead.
Expected measurement depth 39 is explicitly reported for the independent tower schemes.
No classical-vs-quantum asymptotic speedup analysis is provided; only resource tradeoffs are compared.
The 10,000-sample simulation is used to estimate expected depth, not to run a quantum experiment on hardware.
The paper compares T-count and measurement depth between synthesis strategies (53024 vs 28709 vs 45750 T-states per repetition) but does not compare to classical algorithms.
Analysis is purely resource estimation under surface-code assumptions.
